title: Design and analysis of Half-wave and Full-wave Rectifiers
aim: To construct half-wave and full-wave (center-tapped) rectifiers with and without filter capacitor, and to measure ripple factor, efficiency, and load regulation.

theory.summary: Rectifiers convert AC voltage into pulsating DC voltage using diodes that conduct in only one direction. A half-wave rectifier uses a single diode, conducting only during the positive half cycle. A center-tapped full-wave rectifier uses two diodes and a center-tapped transformer, conducting during both half cycles. A capacitor filter connected in parallel with the load resistor smoothens the ripple by charging during the peak of conduction and discharging through the load during non-conduction.

key_formulas.name: Ripple voltage (with filter)
key_formulas.formula: Vr_rms = Idc / (4 * sqrt(3) * f * C) [FW] or Idc / (2 * sqrt(3) * f * C) [HW]
key_formulas.variables: f = source frequency (50Hz), C = filter capacitance

procedure: Step 1: Set up the half-wave rectifier by connecting transformer secondary terminal (9V) to diode anode, cathode to 1kΩ load resistor, and load ground back to transformer center (0V).
Step 2: Connect CRO channel 1 across transformer secondary and channel 2 across load resistor. Measure peak input voltage and peak output voltage.
Step 3: Measure Vdc (using DC voltmeter mode) and Vac (using AC voltmeter mode) across the load. Calculate ripple factor r = Vac / Vdc.
Step 4: Connect a 47μF capacitor in parallel with the load. Measure peak-to-peak ripple voltage on the CRO and calculate ripple factor.
Step 5: Replace 47μF with 100μF filter capacitor and observe ripple waveform changes.
Step 6: Construct the Full-Wave center-tapped rectifier using two 1N4007 diodes. Repeat steps 2 to 5 for the full-wave configuration.

observations.what_to_plot: Input vs Output waveforms on same screen; ripple factor vs load resistance

expected_results.description: Half-wave rectifier should show ripple factor close to 1.21 without filter. Full-wave should show 0.48 without filter. Adding a filter capacitor should drastically drop ripple factor below 0.05. Vdc increases to near Vpeak with filter.

common_errors.symptom: Full-wave rectifier output looks like half-wave (one cycle missing)
common_errors.fix: Verify orientation of both diodes. Silver bands must point towards the same load junction.

common_errors.symptom: Capacitor gets extremely hot or pops
causes: Electrolytic capacitor connected in reverse polarity
common_errors.fix: Always connect the negative stripe side of the capacitor to the ground rail.

causes: Diodes connected back-to-back blocking both cycles
common_errors.fix: Check that the diodes do not oppose each other. Verify transformer voltage with AC multimeter.

circuit_diagnosis_hints: In center-tapped rectifier, both diodes' cathodes must meet at the top of the load resistor.
The ground reference for the CRO probe must be connected to the center-tap wire of the transformer.
A ripple waveform that charges fast and decays slowly is correct. If it decays instantly, the filter capacitor is disconnected.

viva_questions.q: Why is center-tapped FWR peak output voltage less than bridge rectifier output for same transformer rating?
viva_questions.a: Center tap uses only half of the secondary winding at a time, so Vp is half of total secondary peak. Bridge uses full secondary.

viva_questions.q: What is the frequency of ripple in HWR and FWR?
viva_questions.a: Ripple frequency is equal to supply frequency (50Hz) in HWR, and double (100Hz) in FWR.

viva_questions.q: What is Peak Inverse Voltage (PIV) rating and what are the requirements for HWR and FWR?
viva_questions.a: PIV is max voltage diode must withstand when reverse biased. HWR requires PIV >= Vm. Center-tapped FWR requires PIV >= 2Vm.

title: Frequency response of RC Low Pass and High Pass Filters
aim: To construct passive RC low-pass and high-pass filters, measure frequency response, and determine cutoff frequency.

theory.summary: Passive RC filters use resistors and capacitors to pass certain frequencies while attenuating others. A Low-Pass filter passes frequencies below the cutoff frequency fc, where capacitor reactance is high. A High-Pass filter passes frequencies above fc, where capacitor reactance is low. The cutoff frequency fc is the frequency at which the output voltage drops to 70.7% (-3dB) of the input voltage.

key_formulas.name: Cutoff Frequency
key_formulas.variables: R = resistance in ohms, C = capacitance in farads

procedure: Step 1: Construct the Low-Pass Filter — Connect resistor in series with function generator, capacitor in parallel with CRO (across output).
Step 2: Set input amplitude to 2V peak-to-peak. Maintain this input voltage constant throughout the experiment.
Step 3: Vary input frequency from 10Hz to 100kHz. Record output voltage Vo and calculate gain = Vo/Vi and gain in dB = 20 log(Vo/Vi).
Step 4: Construct the High-Pass Filter — Swap the position of the Resistor and Capacitor. Repeat steps 2 and 3.
Step 5: Find fc where gain drops to -3dB (or Vo drops to 1.414V p-p). Compare with theoretical value fc = 1 / (2*pi*R*C).
Step 6: Plot Gain (dB) vs Log Frequency (Bode plot) for both filters on semi-log graph paper.

observations.what_to_plot: Gain in dB on Y-axis vs Log Frequency on X-axis (semi-log graph)

expected_results.description: For R=10kΩ and C=0.01μF, cutoff frequency is ~1591 Hz. Low pass attenuates high frequencies at -20dB/decade. High pass attenuates low frequencies at -20dB/decade. Phase shift is -45° (LP) and +45° (HP) at cutoff.

common_errors.symptom: Cutoff frequency is extremely off from 1.6kHz
causes: Wrong component values read (e.g. 0.1uF capacitor instead of 0.01uF, or 1k resistor instead of 10k)
common_errors.fix: Verify component values using multimeter and capacitor code (103 = 0.01uF).

common_errors.symptom: Output remains equal to input at all frequencies
causes: Output probe connected across input instead of filter components
common_errors.fix: Ensure Channel 2 probe is connected across the capacitor (for LP) or resistor (for HP) and not across the function generator.

circuit_diagnosis_hints: In Low Pass: Resistor connects from input to output node. Capacitor connects from output node to ground.
In High Pass: Capacitor connects from input to output node. Resistor connects from output node to ground.

viva_questions.q: What is the roll-off rate of a single-stage RC filter?
viva_questions.a: -20 dB/decade (or -6 dB/octave). It means the gain drops by 20dB for every 10-fold increase in frequency beyond cutoff.

viva_questions.q: What is the phase shift at the cutoff frequency for LP and HP filters?
viva_questions.a: -45 degrees for Low Pass (output lags input) and +45 degrees for High Pass (output leads input).

viva_questions.q: Why is it called a passive filter?
viva_questions.a: It uses only passive components (resistors, capacitors) and does not require external DC power supplies or provide voltage amplification.

title: Design of RC Phase-Shift Oscillator
aim: To design and test an RC phase-shift oscillator using an op-amp, and measure output frequency and starting gain requirements.

theory.summary: An oscillator is an amplifier with positive feedback that generates a periodic AC signal without an external input. The Barkhausen criteria require loop gain Aβ = 1 and phase shift around loop = 0 or 360 degrees. An RC phase-shift oscillator uses three RC stages in feedback loop. Each RC stage is designed to provide 60 degrees phase shift at the oscillation frequency, totaling 180 degrees. The inverting op-amp amplifier provides the remaining 180 degrees phase shift. The feedback attenuation factor β is 1/29, so the op-amp closed-loop gain must be at least 29 (Rf/R >= 29) to sustain oscillations.

key_formulas.name: Frequency of Oscillation
key_formulas.variables: R = phase shift resistor, C = phase shift capacitor

key_formulas.name: Required Gain
key_formulas.variables: Rf = feedback resistor, R = input resistor

procedure: Step 1: Set up the inverting amplifier stage using LM741 with R1=10kΩ, Rf=290kΩ (or 330kΩ pot). Connect ±12V supplies.
Step 2: Connect the three-stage RC feedback ladder: connect output pin 6 to first RC, then second, then third RC output back to the inverting input (pin 2).
Step 3: Connect the non-inverting input (pin 3) to ground.
Step 4: Connect CRO to the output pin 6. Power on the dual supply.
Step 5: Adjust the Rf pot until sustained sinusoidal oscillations appear on the screen. If oscillations don't start, increase Rf.
Step 6: Measure the output frequency and amplitude on the CRO. Compare with the theoretical frequency fo = 1 / (2*pi*R*C*sqrt(6)).

observations.what_to_plot: Sine wave output waveform showing amplitude and time period

expected_results.description: Output should be a clean sine wave. For R=10kΩ and C=0.01μF, the frequency of oscillation is ~650Hz. Oscillation starts when Rf is adjusted slightly above 290kΩ (gain > 29) due to loading.

causes: Rf pot value is too low (gain < 29)
One of the RC stages is wired incorrectly
Op-amp dual supply missing negative rail
common_errors.fix: Increase Rf potentiometer resistance. Check connection of the 3 RC stages back to pin 2. Verify ±12V supplies.

common_errors.symptom: Output is a clipped sine wave or square wave
causes: Rf set too high causing op-amp to saturate to the rails
common_errors.fix: Slightly reduce the Rf potentiometer resistance until the output becomes a clean, undistorted sine wave.

circuit_diagnosis_hints: The three capacitors must be in series in the feedback path, with resistors going to ground.
Ensure the third RC stage resistor is actually the input resistor R1 connected to pin 2 (the virtual ground).

viva_questions.q: Why is Rf/R required to be at least 29?
viva_questions.a: The three-stage RC feedback network attenuates the signal by a factor of 1/29 at the frequency where phase shift is 180 degrees. To maintain loop gain Aβ = 1, amplifier gain A must be >= 29.

viva_questions.q: What is the advantage of RC phase-shift oscillator?
viva_questions.a: It is simple to design, requires no inductors (excellent for low frequencies), and produces a very stable, low-distortion sine wave.

viva_questions.q: Why is it not suitable for high frequency range?
viva_questions.a: Frequency tuning is difficult because all three capacitors or resistors must be changed simultaneously. Frequency stability is lower at high frequencies due to loading.

title: Design of Wien Bridge Oscillator
aim: To design and test a Wien Bridge oscillator using an op-amp, measure output frequency, and verify gain requirements.

theory.summary: A Wien Bridge oscillator is a highly stable oscillator used to generate audio frequencies. It uses a lead-lag bridge network in the feedback path. The lead-lag network acts as a band-pass filter with zero phase shift and maximum transmission (β = 1/3) at the resonant frequency fo. To satisfy Barkhausen criteria, the amplifier must be non-inverting with zero phase shift and closed-loop gain Av = 1 + Rf/R1 = 3 (so Rf/R1 >= 2). A diode limiter or thermistor is often added to the feedback path for amplitude stabilization.

key_formulas.name: Resonant Frequency
key_formulas.variables: Assuming equal R and C in lead-lag branches

procedure: Step 1: Construct the non-inverting amplifier stage using LM741. Connect R1=10kΩ from pin 2 to ground, Rf=20kΩ pot from pin 2 to output pin 6.
Step 2: Connect the lead-lag feedback network: series RC (R=10k, C=0.01u) from output pin 6 to non-inverting input pin 3. Parallel RC (R=10k, C=0.01u) from pin 3 to ground.
Step 3: Turn on the ±12V power supply. Observe the output waveform on CRO.
Step 4: Slowly increase Rf pot from minimum. Note the point where sinusoidal oscillations begin.
Step 5: Measure output frequency and amplitude. Compare with theoretical value fo = 1 / (2*pi*R*C).
Step 6: Observe clipping/saturation when Rf is turned further up.

observations.what_to_plot: Sinusoidal output wave showing resonant frequency

expected_results.description: Clean sinusoidal oscillations at ~1.59kHz for R=10kΩ and C=0.01μF. Oscillations sustain when Rf is slightly above 20kΩ (Av >= 3).

causes: Lead-lag network connected to inverting input pin 2 instead of non-inverting pin 3
common_errors.fix: Increase Rf pot. Ensure feedback network goes to pin 3 (positive feedback). R1/Rf feedback goes to pin 2 (negative feedback).

common_errors.symptom: Oscillations start but decay to zero
causes: Gain is exactly 3 but loading drops it
common_errors.fix: Slightly increase Rf pot above 20kΩ to force startup, then use diode amplitude limiting if distortion is too high.

circuit_diagnosis_hints: The series R-C connects output to pin 3. The parallel R-C connects pin 3 to ground. The negative feedback divider R1-Rf connects to pin 2.

viva_questions.q: What is the advantage of Wien Bridge oscillator over RC phase shift?
viva_questions.a: Frequency can be varied easily by using a dual-ganged variable resistor. It provides a cleaner sine wave and better frequency stability.

viva_questions.q: Why is the feedback attenuation factor (β) equal to 1/3?
viva_questions.a: At resonant frequency, reactances of series and parallel RC are equal, resulting in output voltage across parallel RC being exactly 1/3 of input and in phase.

viva_questions.q: What is the purpose of amplitude stabilization in oscillators?
viva_questions.a: To prevent output amplitude from growing exponentially and clipping due to transistor/op-amp saturation. It dynamically adjusts gain to exactly 3.
